Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Describe anatomic details of the extensor mechanism.
List the zones of injury for extensor tendon injuries.
Recognize the clinical presentation of patients with an extensor tendon injury.
Determine nonsurgical and surgical treatment options for the management of extensor
tendon injuries.
Identify the complications of the management of extensor tendon injuries.

Injuries of the hand result in 10% of all emergency department visits (Resources 1 and 2).
Higher risk in men and individuals aged 20 to 29 years
Laceration with a knife/glass is the most common mechanism of injury (saw injury is second
most common).
Extensor tendon injuries occur more frequently than flexor tendon injuries.
Work injury in approximately 25% of patients1,2
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Biomechanics
Tendons have viscoelastic properties
Viscoelastic: property of a material that exhibits viscous and elastic characteristics during
deformation
Viscoelastic materials demonstrate properties dependent on the rate at which a force is
applied. At a low loading rate, a tendon is compliant but becomes increasingly stiff with an
increasing load rate.
Blix curve
Length (x-axis) and tension (y-axis) plots the integrated components of active contraction and
elastic recoil of a muscle-tendon unit.
The greatest contractile force is exerted if a muscle is at its resting length.
Important consideration for identifying the optimal myotendinous tension, particularly as it
relates to tendon transfers or myotendinous level forearm extensor injuries
Tendon excursion
Most extensor tendon excursion occurs at the forearm, wrist, and dorsal hand (not much
over the digital level).
Amplitude of extensor excursion3
Amplitude of wrist extensor excursion is 3.3 cm.
Amplitude of digital and thumb extensor excursion proximally is 5 cm, whereas the
terminal extensor tendon is only 1 to 2 mm.
In comparison, the digital and thumb flexors have approximately 7 cm of amplitude of
excursion.
Tendon gliding
Related to tendon excursion; tendon gliding is the ability of a tendon to move without excess
resistance.

Scar adhesions limit tendon gliding.
Impaired tendon gliding may occur with or without concomitant joint contractures.
The flat nature of the extensor tendons at the digital level in combination with their close
proximity with the proximal, middle, and distal phalanges place these tendons at risk for
impaired tendon gliding postinjury.
Vascular Anatomy
Dissimilar from the flexor tendons, the extensor tendons do not have vincula.
Intrinsic blood supply occurs at the musculotendinous/osteotendinous junctions.
Extrinsic blood supply occurs through the mesotenon and supplies the midportion of the
tendon.
Neural Anatomy
Myelinated: specialized mechanoreceptors (Golgi tendon organs) sense tension and pressure
in the tendon
Unmyelinated: sense and transmission of pain (nociceptors)
Tendons
Tendon structure
Tendons are organized groups of fascicles containing longitudinally oriented bundles of
collagen (primarily type I) and fibroblasts called tenocytes.
Individual fascicles are covered by endotenon.
Epitenon covers groups of tendon fascicles.
Visceral and parietal paratenons line the surface of the tendon and the undersurface of the
tendon sheath, respectively.
Extensor tendon nutrition
At the level of the wrist joint, extensor tendon nutrition is accomplished via an extrinsic
mechanism through diffusion from vessels in the mesotenon, which spans the length of the
extensor retinaculum.
Distally, the extensor tendons are covered by the paratenon.
With a dorsal digital avulsion injury, stripping of the paratenon negatively affects the
success of skin grafting and necessitates the need for adipofascial coverage.
Small segmental vessels from the paratenon supply the tendon distal to the retinaculum.

An illustration of extensor tendon anatomy is shown in Figure 1.
Figure 1 Lateral (A) and dorsal (B) view illustrations show the extensor mechanism anatomy
of the finger. DIP = distal interphalangeal joint, MCP = metacarpophalangeal joint, ORL =
oblique retinacular ligament, PIP = proximal interphalangeal joint, TRL = transverse
retinacular ligament. (Adapted with permission from Coons MS, Green SM: Boutonniere
deformity. Hand Clin 1995;11[3]:387-402.)
Tendon healing
Phases of tendon healing
Inflammatory phase (time of injury to 7 days postinjury)—Fibroblast and macrophage
migration to the site of injury results in phagocytosis of the clot and necrotic tissue. During
this phase, repair strength relies entirely on the strength of the suture used.
Proliferative phase (weeks 1 to 3 postinjury)—Neovascularization begins. An increasing
number of fibroblasts deposit immature type III collagen, which is later replaced by type I
collagen. Tendon repairs do not accrue tensile strength until the beginning of the remodeling
phase.
Remodeling phase (weeks 3 to 12 postinjury)—Collagen fibers become organized along the
length of the tendon.
Mechanisms of tendon healing
Extrinsic tendon healing involves inflammatory cells and fibroblasts derived from the tendon
sheath and predominates with immobilization of the repaired tendon. Collagen deposition is

Intrinsic tendon healing is accomplished via inflammatory cells and fibroblasts derived from
within the tendon and the epitenon. The intrinsic mechanism predominates if motion
rehabilitation is used postoperatively.
Biochemistry of tendon healing (see flexor tendon chapter)
Anatomic Considerations
Extensor retinaculum4 (Resource 3 and 4; Figures 2 and 3)
Keeps the extensor tendons in place, acting as a pulley to prevent bowstringing
Six separate dorsal extensor fibro-osseous compartments are present at the wrist.
Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis
Extensor carpi radialis longus and extensor carpi radialis brevis
Extensor pollicis longus
Extensor digitorum communis (EDC) and extensor indicis proprius (EIP)
Extensor digiti minimi or extensor digiti quinti (EDQ)
Extensor carpi ulnaris

metacarpophalangeal joint. The sagittal band arises from the volar plate and the
intermetacarpal ligament and stabilizes the extensor tendon. DIP = distal interphalangeal, MP
= metacarpophalangeal, PIP = proximal interphalangeal. (Reproduced from Kleinhenz BP,

metacarpophalangeal joint. DIP = distal interphalangeal, MP = metacarpophalangeal, PIP =

Intrinsic/extrinsic components of digital movement
Digital metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint extension occurs via pull of the extrinsic digital
extensors (EDC, EIP, and EDQ) through the sagittal band fibers.
Digital proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint extension occurs through the central slip, which is a
blend of fibers from the lateral bands (intrinsic components from the volar/dorsal interossei
and lumbrical) and the common central extensor (derived from the extrinsic tendon
contribution, namely the EDC, EIP, and EDQ).

6/23

Digital distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint extension occurs through the terminal tendon, which
consists of the conjoined lateral bands (intrinsic mechanism) over the middle phalanx level.
Oblique retinacular ligament
Passive structure that coordinates interphalangeal extension
Proximal attachment is volarly located at the PIP joint volar plate and flexor sheath near the
PIP joint
Distal attachment is dorsally at the lateral aspects of the terminal tendon.
If this structure is tight postinjury, passive DIP joint flexion will be limited, with blocking of the
PIP joint in extension.
Lateral bands
Composite of intrinsic contribution that develops at radial and ulnar aspects of the proximal
phalanges distal to the sagittal bands (the lumbrical is only present radially with a variable
innervation—the index and long fingers from the median nerve and the ring and little fingers
from the ulnar nerve)
Stabilized radially and ulnarly by the retinacular ligaments at the PIP joint level
Stabilized distal to the central slip by the triangular ligament, which, if incompetent, leads to
separation of the lateral bands over the middle phalanx level (contributing feature of a
boutonnière deformity)
Contracture/tightness of the retinacular ligaments draws the lateral bands volar, resulting in
PIP joint flexion and DIP joint hyperextension deformities (boutonnière deformity).
Laxity/insufficiency of the retinacular ligaments draws the lateral bands dorsal, resulting in
PIP joint hyperextension and DIP joint flexion (swan-neck deformity).5
Junctura tendinae
Provide stability between the EDC tendons at the distal metacarpal level, proximal to the
MCP joints
Typically, three common junctura tendinum attachments are oriented in oblique vectors.
EDC long finger proximal to EDC index finger distal
EDC ring finger proximal to EDC long finger distal
EDC ring finger proximal to EDC little finger distal
Intact juctura tendinae play a clinical role with zone 6 extensor injuries.
Specifically, even with a laceration in zone 6, an intact junctura may allow for continued
digital extension via tendon pull through the junctura to the adjacent intact tendon.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:20 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002069

Zone I (mallet finger)
The mechanism of injury resulting in an acute loss of active extension of the DIP joint may be
a blunt injury (eg, a baseball or football striking and forcibly passively flexing the DIP joint) or
a sharp (laceration) injury to the terminal extensor insertion.
With a hyperextensible PIP joint, a mallet injury may instead present as a swan-neck
deformity, in which the lateral bands are notably more dorsal, accentuating PIP joint
hyperextension along with the extensor lag from the primary mallet injury at the DIP joint
Zone II (injury over the middle phalanx level)
Typically from laceration or other penetrating trauma
Zone III injuries (acute boutonnière deformity)
Acute loss of PIP joint extension results from injury to the central slip of the extensor
apparatus at or just proximal to the level of the PIP joint.
Palmar PIP joint dislocations (often with a bony avulsion at the central slip) and lacerations
over the dorsum of the PIP joint are the most common mechanisms of injury.
Progressive volar subluxation of the lateral bands may cause DIP joint extension in
combination with a PIP joint flexion deformity, resulting in the boutonnière deformity.
Injury Classification
Level of Injury
Nine extensor zones are present in the hand, wrist, and forearm and are used to identify the
level of injury 6 - 8 ( Figures 4 and 5 ).
Zone I: finger, DIP joint level; thumb, interphalangeal level
Zone II: finger, middle phalanx level; thumb, proximal phalanx level
Zone III: Finger, PIP joint level; thumb, MCP joint level
Zone IV: Finger, proximal phalanx level; thumb, metacarpal level
Zone V: Finger, MCP joint level; thumb, carpometacarpal/radial styloid level
Zone VI: Finger, metacarpal level
Zone VII: Finger, extensor retinaculum
Zone VIII: Finger, distal forearm
Zone IX: Finger, middle/proximal forearm
At the digital level, the odd number zones are over the joints (zone I, DIP joint; zone III, PIP
joint; zone V, MCP joint)

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Mechanism of injury affects management.
A crush injury with extensor disruption should indicate possible additional injury to the
joints/bones in proximity to the extensor injury and the flexor sheath (ie, full-thickness
injury).
A laceration typically results in a more defined level of the zone of injury and associated
structures.
Physical Examination
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:20 PM
AAOS | Hand and Wrist Extensor Tendon Repair and Reconstruction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002069
10/23

Physical examination of the injured hand
The physical examination should begin with observation of the resting position of the hand
and assessment of the digital cascade.
Malalignment or malrotation of the digits may be a sign of an underlying fracture.
A neurovascular examination should be performed given the proximity of the tendons,
particularly the flexors, to the digital neurovascular bundles.
Assessment of skin integrity on the dorsal and palmar aspects of the hand helps localize
potential sites of tendon injury.
Lacerations near joints must be carefully inspected for evidence of traumatic arthrotomy
(Video 1)
Physical examination and classification of extensor tendon injuries
Zone I and zone II extensor tendon injuries involve the terminal insertion of the extensor
mechanism and result in the finger assuming a flexed posture of the DIP joint, or mallet
finger.
The patient is unable to actively extend the DIP joint.
Open injuries in this zone involve transection of the tendon, whereas closed injuries in this
zone may involve a bony avulsion from the dorsal base of the distal phalanx and
necessitate radiographic evaluation.

Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2016, pp 432.
Imaging Studies
Radiographs are useful to assess bony avulsion injuries, associated fractures/dislocations,
and/or foreign bodies.
With a dorsal digital crush mechanism of injury, a fracture indicates an associated full-
thickness soft-tissue injury involving the extensor mechanism.
MRI/CT usually are not indicated in patients with a digital extensor injury but may have a role
in patients with a more proximally located lesion if clinical uncertainty exists.
Ultrasonography may be useful for a sagittal band injury with extensor subluxation; however,
clinical examination often is sufficient to make the diagnosis.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Dissimilar from an open injury, a closed injury typically is more amenable to nonsurgical
management.
Zone I and zone III closed ruptures generally are managed nonsurgically.
Zone V closed injuries (ie, sagittal band rupture) also can be managed nonsurgically (at least
initially).
Partial tendon lacerations may be considered for nonsurgical management; although
controversial, some studies suggest that as much as 90% of a tendon can be lacerated and still
be managed nonsurgically.
Contraindications
Combined injuries involving fracture/dislocation benefit from stable fracture fixation and
extensor tendon repair to allow for motion exercises to limit scar formation.
Open/contaminated wounds are managed surgically.

Techniques/Procedures
Zone I (closed injury)
Most closed injuries are managed via full-time extension splinting of the DIP joint for 6 to 8
weeks. The role of subsequent nighttime or sport-time splinting is a subject of debate, with
some recommending a subsequent 4-week period of splinting at night or during sporting
activities.11
Alumafoam, thermoplast, and multiple other splinting materials are associated with similar
outcomes.
Serial cast immobilization has appeal with respect to compliance of management.
Percutaneous trans-articular pinning may be considered in certain patient populations (eg,
healthcare professionals) but is associated with a risk of local/deep infection and
catastrophic hardware breakage12 (Resource 5).
Zone III (closed injury)
Most closed injuries are managed via full-time extension splinting of the DIP joint for 6 to 8
weeks, followed by several weeks of night splinting.
Similar to zone I, multiple splint options are available to facilitate maintenance of full-time
PIP joint extension.
Serial cast immobilization has appeal with respect to facilitating reduction of fusiform
swelling and maintaining PIP joint correction.
Emphasis on lateral band mobilization via passive DIP joint flexion is a necessary component
of management to facilitate terminal tendon gliding and stretching of the oblique retinacular
ligament.
Relative motion splinting in which MCP joint of the involved digit is maintained flexed relative
to the adjacent digits may be a reasonable alternative13 (Resource 6).
Zone V (closed injury)
Correction of the deviated digit and immobilization of the MCP joint in extension are
necessary for a sagittal band rupture.
Traditionally, use of outrigger splints with slings allowing short-arc MCP joint motion have
been used.
Relative motion splinting in which the MCP joint of the involved digit is maintained extended
relative to the adjacent digits is quickly becoming a favored treatment option for closed
management of a sagittal band rupture because it is effective and less cumbersome (Figure
6).

Pitfalls and Preventive Measures
Equally important to the quality of the tendon repair is the status of the wound bed and soft-
tissue coverage. Both are important in terms of outcome to facilitate tendon gliding and
minimization of adhesions.
Limitation of DIP joint flexion is a concern after repair of a zone I or zone II injury. This is
because of the following considerations associated with these injuries:
High risk for subdermal tendon adhesions because of a minimal adipo-fascial soft-tissue
envelope
Close proximity of the injury to the DIP joint, creating a higher risk for joint contracture
Tenorrhaphy quality is diminished because of the flat nature of the tendon and limited ability
to use core suture techniques.
The terminal position of the repair site in reference to the remainder of the digit diminishes
the fulcrum on which active tendon gliding can occur.
Zone V and zone VI injuries may be missed given the accessory extensor force created via an
intact junctura tendinum, which may somewhat conceal a primary complete extensor
laceration.
Placement of the wrist passively into extension and then having the patient actively extend
the MCP joint may facilitate more accurate evaluation of tendon integrity at this level.

Use of passive wrist tenodesis with flexion may yield a picture of preserved MCP joint
extension through the junctura tendinum, disguising the tendon laceration and leading to a
missed injury.
Pseudo-boutonnière deformity
May result from a hyperextension injury to the PIP joint, spraining the volar plate and one
or both collateral ligaments
The tendon is intact; rather, PIP joint flexion is present because of capsular contracture
rather than central slip tendon injury.
The presence of fusiform swelling in a patient reluctant to undergo physical examination
yields a boutonnière-like deformity and incorrect diagnosis of a central slip injury.
Dissimilar from a true boutonnière deformity, a pseudo-boutonnière deformity will not
result in DIP joint hyperextension.
Use of the Elson test to assess active PIP joint extension against resistance is important in
distinguishing this injury. In patients with a flexion contracture related to a joint injury
(occasionally referred to as a pseudo-boutonnière injury), transfer of force through the
lateral bands will not occur during this maneuver, resulting in a lax/floppy DIP joint.
Complications
Pain
In some patients, mallet injuries may result in ongoing pain for 6 to 12 months postinjury.
Patients with persistent pain after a crush injury who have an associated extensor disruption
should be evaluated for an occult osteochondral articular injury.
A patient with an extensor injury complicated by considerable post-injury swelling may be at
risk for adhesions and persistent pain.
Infection
The overall infection rate for an extensor laceration is low because of the relative superficial
location of the wound bed, enabling more successful initial efforts to irrigate the injury.
Grossly contaminated wounds, large open wounds, or more severe crush injuries are at higher
risk of posttraumatic residual and should be urgently taken to the operating room for
thorough débridement. Staged soft-tissue coverage and later repair of the tendon injury may
need to be considered.

Dog/cat bite injuries with extensor involvement require the use of prophylactic antibiotic
agents (such as amoxicillin/clavulanate or ciprofloxacin and clindamycin) in combination with
very close outpatient follow-up because of the high risk of bacterial inoculation.
Digital extensor lacerations that are clean and not the result of mechanism of injury in which
contamination was present have been shown to result in good outcomes, even without the
use of prophylactic antibiotic agents.
Identification of a traumatic MCP joint arthrotomy in patients with a zone IV, zone V, or VI
injury (especially with a fight bite injury) is paramount to decrease the risk of posttraumatic
infection.
Tendon Rupture After Repair
Predisposing factors include inadequate suture material, inadequate surgical technique,
suboptimal postoperative rehabilitation, and noncompliance.
Acute recognition and timely exploration may allow for revision repair under ideal
circumstances.
Tendon reconstruction is preferred for the management of late rupture and ruptures
associated with excessive scarring (free autograft or turndown graft are considered).
Re-rupture most frequently occurs during the first 7 to 10 days postoperatively.
Composite circumferential digital injuries that involve the flexor and extensor tendons create a
challenge with postoperative physical therapy because of the antagonistic rehabilitation
principles necessary for each injury. This may place the extensor tendon at greater risk for a
repair gap given the primary goal of recovery of grasp.
Tendon Adhesions
Despite advances in tendon repair rehabilitation, adhesion formation remains the one of the
most common complications after extensor tendon repair.
Factors associated with increased adhesion formation include extensive crush injuries,
excessive surgical manipulation, associated fractures and infections, and reconstruction of
failed primary repair.
Dynamic splinting (use of elastic traction to stretch tissues) and static progressive splinting
(three-point force translation with progressive change in the splint positioning through a gear)
may be used in the recovery of flexibility for a stiff digit.

If a substantial difference exists between the active and passive motion of a digit despite
dedicated efforts in physical therapy, adhesion release or tenolysis is considered.
Tenolysis16 (Resource 9)
Indications—The ideal candidate for tenolysis is a patient with localized tendon adhesions,
minimal to no joint contracture, and full passive digital motion who is motivated to perform
immediate postoperative physical therapy.
Tenolysis in combination with other procedures that would require postoperative
immobilization (eg, nerve repair, local flap coverage, or bone grafting) is discouraged.
Generally, tenolysis is performed no earlier than 3 to 6 months after tendon repair.
Restoration of motion may be easier to assess by performing tenolysis under local
anesthesia, with the patient awake and moving their hand.
Dorsal, dorsolateral, and midlateral incisions are favored surgical approaches.
Extrinsic tightness
A laceration at zone V, zone VI, or zone VII may lead to adhesions that create limited digital
flexion because of tethering of the digit.
This is noted if differentially less active/passive PIP joint flexion is present with positioning of
the MCP joint in flexion compared with extension.
Extensor tenolysis is used to correct this problem.
Intrinsic tightness
A laceration at zone IV (particularly if more laterally through the lateral band) may lead to
adhesions or tendon shortening, limiting digital flexion.
This is noted if differentially less active/passive PIP joint flexion is present with positioning of
the MCP joint in extension compared with flexion (Bunnell intrinsic tightness test)
Intrinsic releases (tenotomies performed through the intrinsic tendons on the radial and ulnar
aspects of the proximal phalanx level) are performed to correct this issue.
Joint Contracture
Concomitant DIP joint contracture is highest with zone I and zone II injuries, whereas
concomitant PIP joint contracture is highest with zone III and zone IV injuries.
Early identification, stretching exercises, and splinting (perhaps via formal physical therapy)
may help manage developing contracture.
Surgical management is an option if residual contracture limits function.

The surgical technique involves dorsal capsulectomy and possible sequential dorsal-to-palmar
collateral ligament release.
Capsulectomy typically is performed in combination with extensor tenolysis17 (Resource 10).
Late Complications
Chronic boutonnière deformity
If not managed acutely, a central slip injury results in the following:
Disruption of the triangular ligament, which disengages the lateral bands from their
balanced position.
The lateral bands subluxate volarly, which leads to an increased flexion moment at the PIP
joint. This subluxation is further accentuated via contracture of the transverse retinacular
ligaments.
Increased tension on the lateral bands translates to the terminal tendon, resulting in DIP
joint hyperextension.
Initially, a boutonnière deformity may be passively correctable and, therefore, amenable to
physical therapy. This may progress to a fixed contracture in which, ultimately the PIP joint
volar plate and the collateral ligament become contracted.
Surgical treatment options depend on whether the joint is contracted. Joint contraction must
be corrected before performing any tendon procedures (PIP joint volar plate release).
Tendon procedures include:
Release of the contracted transverse retinacular ligaments to allow for dorsal mobilization
of the lateral bands
Central slip secondary repair or tendon graft reconstruction (alternative: Littler
reconstruction—lateral band transection and repair to the central slip insertion)
Tenolysis of the lateral bands and the terminal tendon to facilitate DIP joint flexion
An alternative to recover DIP joint flexion in a patient with a chronic boutonnière deformity
includes a Dolphin/modified Fowler terminal tenotomy, achieved via oblique terminal tendon
release distal to the central slip18 (Resource 11).
Late swan-neck deformity
A chronic mallet injury may result in a secondary swan-neck deformity (more commonly
observed in patients with generalized hyperlaxity).
Force translation back at the PIP joint level occurs after loss of terminal tendon integrity,
resulting in PIP joint hyperextension.

9/3/26, 4:20 PM
AAOS | Hand and Wrist Extensor Tendon Repair and Reconstruction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002069
18/23

This results in contracture of the triangular ligament and subsequent dorsal subluxation of
the lateral bands (adding to PIP joint hyperextension force).
Surgical treatment options include:
Removal of scar at the terminal tendon/secondary repair
Central slip tenotomy—Involves a dorsal or midlateral incision to access and release the
central slip beneath the extensor mechanism. This eliminates the PIP joint extension force,
which is translated distally to the terminal tendon through the lateral bands.19
Spiral oblique retinacular ligament reconstruction
Corrective recovery of DIP joint extension and PIP joint flexion
Involves the use of a palmaris longus tendon graft fixed to the terminal tendon insertion,
which is then passed in a spiral fashion volarly between the flexor tendons and the PIP
joint and then fixed to the lateral cortex of the proximal phalanx (bone tunnel with the
use of a button or interference screw).
Selective joint arthrodesis may be considered as an option late treatment, especially in
patients with traumatic arthropathy or severe joint fibrosis.
Pearls and Pitfalls
Status of the soft-tissue envelope may be the key factor in management and prognosis,
including recovery of motion in zone I through IV injuries.
Adhesions between the repair site and the surrounding tissues is the most common
complication associated with an extensor tendon injury.
An understanding of the complex interplay between the intrinsic and extrinsic components of
the extensor mechanism is paramount to a successful rehabilitation program.
Repair of an extensor tendon in the emergency department should be discouraged because
meticulous soft-tissue handling and proper suture technique are necessary.
Beware of injuries suspicious for a human bite mechanism of injury.
Recognize the difference between a true central slip injury and a pseudo-boutonnière injury.11
